newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: MPS shows NZ economy in drift, not drive - Cullen.
newsitem.headline: MPS shows NZ economy in drift, not drive - Cullen.

text.p: The general impression to be gained from the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's Monetary Policy Statement (MPS), delivered on Friday, was of an economy and a government in a state of drift rather than drive, opposition Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen said.
He said the MPS endorsed the view that growth over the next year or two would be largely driven by domestic demand rather than by export growth.
"This is increasingly the area where Labour has its greatest concerns about the present path of economic management," Cullen said.

"Further analysis of yesterday's Budget shows an appalling lack of investment in key elements crucial to the development of an internationally competitive economy. Infrastructure, training and export development were all big losers in yesterday's budget."
This meant there was no coherent strategy to provide for a sustainable lift in New Zealand's economic performance over the medium term, Cullen said.

"Even within this lack of direction there has to be concern about the very small room for manoeuvre the goverment has left itself. Any significant shortfall in growth will leave it facing hard choices which, on the basis of yesterday's Budget, it does not have the capacity politically to address."
Cullen said there would be no significant fall in either interest rates of the exchange rate as a result of the MPS.
"The Reserve Bank's desired monetary conditions in this statement were exactly as they actually were moments before the statement was released," he said.
"This means that while there may be some small reduction in the exchange rate, the level of movement may not be sufficient to give major relief to manufacturers, farmers and exporters."
The Reserve Bank sanctioned a 100 basis point easing in monetary conditions from the levels it desired in its March Economic Projections.
But because the financial markets had already loosened conditions to that level and beyond, the bank said it was not seeking any further easing in actual conditions.
